newsitem.title: UK: Water companies under attack at UK drought summit.
newsitem.headline: Water companies under attack at UK drought summit.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government warned water companies on Monday it would impose tough regulations to ensure water supplies were used efficiently to counter the country's worst drought in 200 years.

At a "crisis summit" of water concerns, regulators and environmental and consumer lobbyists, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said he would be firm with an industry already facing a windfall tax on profits after Labour's May 1 election victory.
"I think the public want me to talk tough. There's been enough talk of crisis management short-term and (that) this problem will soon go away if the rain comes back," Prescott said.
"It's (water) not being used efficiently and effectively and what we've got to do is bring in the proper regulatory form and to be quite tough with the industry."

Britain, famous for its rain and drizzle, is weathering its driest two-year spell since the mid-18th century. The first four months of 1997 were the driest start to the year in England and Wales since 1929.
Labour has been sharply critical of the water companies since they were privatised at the turn of the decade by the previous Conservative government.
Worsening drought conditions have been compounded by leakage of huge amounts of water from broken pipes and many Britons wound up banned from watering their lawns and gardens last year.
But at the same time, privatised companies were paying out hefty dividends to shareholders and fat pay packets to executives.
Widespread public anger resulted, contributing to the Conservatives' crushing defeat at the polls three weeks ago.
Prescott said he proposed a 10-point plan for the water industry, including a five-year target to cut leaks and improved compensation for customers hit by shortages.
OFWAT, regulator for the water industry, added to the pressure on companies by saying it would set mandatory targets to reduce leakages for 1998-99 in the autumn.
Shares in water companies fell on the stock exchange following the OFWAT statement with Thames Water leading, down 13.5 pence to 672. Thames loses 38 percent of all treated water going into pipes.
Some experts say about 800 million gallons (3.64 billion litres) a day are lost through pipes. This year companies will try to cut leakages by 150 million a day to conform to OFWAT demands.
Prescott told a news conference it would be prepared to look at extra powers for OFWAT to ensure mandatory leakage targets were met. "We will watch what happens over the summer," he said.
The industry maintains that it has invested more than 500 million pounds ($820 million) on drought-related measures.
Companies say Britons should begin to treat water as a precious resource through measures such as metering or higher tariffs for non-essential use in gardens and swimming pools.
Labour's windfall tax on privatised utilities will be used for a programme to put 250,000 unemployed young people to work. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
